overview.text: In economics, a monopoly is a market structure in which one seller is the sole supplier of a product with no close substitutes, giving it meaningful influence over price rather than forcing it to accept a market price. Its power often persists because barriers—such as legal protections, control of a key resource, or high fixed costs—make entry difficult. Unlike a firm in perfect competition, a monopolist chooses output with the market demand curve in view; standard models predict it may restrict output and charge more than a competitive market, creating inefficiency. In antitrust law, “monopoly” can refer more broadly to durable market power, and dominance alone is not automatically illegal.

key_facts.text: A monopoly differs from an oligopoly: the monopoly model has one supplier, while an oligopoly has a few competing firms.
Barriers to entry can include legal restrictions, control of a scarce resource, and cost advantages from economies of scale.
A natural monopoly may arise when one provider can serve a market at lower average cost than multiple providers duplicating costly infrastructure, such as water pipes.
In the standard economic model, a monopolist faces the market demand curve; unlike a competitive firm, it does not simply take the market price as given.
U.S. antitrust analysis distinguishes having a leading position from illegally maintaining monopoly power: courts examine market conditions and whether conduct improperly excludes competitors.
